think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 55-year-old patient from an endemic region presents with 6 months of chronic left hypochondrial pain and is found to have a large 12-cm retroperitoneal mass in the upper pole of the left kidney contiguous with the left adrenal gland. In an adult, a solitary large adrenal/retroperitoneal mass typically represents an adrenocortical carcinoma, a functioning pheochromocytoma, or an adrenal cyst. Furthermore, serum echinococcal IgM and IgG serology was completely negative, creating significant diagnostic ambiguity prior to surgical exploration.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The presentation concludes following outpatient clinical history, normal physical examination and blood pressure, initial laboratory tests (CBC, normal 24-hour urinary VMA and metanephrines), and baseline abdominal ultrasonography showing a large hypoechoic retroperitoneal mass in the upper pole of the left kidney with cystic components, immediately prior to send-out serology, CT imaging, and surgical laparotomy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pheochromocytoma / functional adrenal medullary tumor was a key consideration due to the suprarenal adrenal mass, but arterial blood pressure was normal and 24-hour urinary metanephrines and VMA were within normal ranges. Adrenocortical carcinoma or retroperitoneal sarcoma was considered given the 12-cm mass diameter, but abdominal CT demonstrated a sharply circumscribed, multicystic lesion with scattered calcifications and lack of retroperitoneal fat invasion or venous thrombus. Echinococcal seronegativity occurs in encapsulated, calcified, or quiescent cysts, necessitating operative pathology for final confirmation.
case_prompt: A 55-year-old patient living in a rural endemic area is referred for hospital evaluation of dull left hypochondrial pain evolving over the preceding 6 months, without associated nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. The patient has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On physical examination, arterial blood pressure is normal, and abdominal examination reveals no palpable abdominal tenderness or organomegaly. Baseline laboratory evaluation including a complete blood count is entirely normal. Twenty-four-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and fractionated metanephrine levels are within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals a large hypoechoic retroperitoneal mass located in the upper pole of the left kidney containing internal cystic components.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A large retroperitoneal mass closely associated with the adrenal gland prompted evaluation for a catecholamine-producing pheochromocytoma, but arterial blood pressure was normal and 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and metanephrines were entirely within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Arterial blood pressure was within normal limits... Blood analysis including complete blood count, 24-h urinary VMA and metanephrine were normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A 12-cm adrenal mass in an adult raises strong suspicion for primary adrenocortical carcinoma or sarcoma, but cross-sectional CT revealed a sharply circumscribed, multicystic architecture with scattered calcifications and complete absence of perirenal fat infiltration or vascular invasion.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The CT scan showed a well-circumscribed non-enhanced multi-cystic 12 cm mass with scattered calcifications located above the left kidney and the left adrenal gland which seemed shadowed (Fig. 1). The mass has a compressive effect on the adjacent organs with no perirenal or adrenal fat infiltration, no invasion of thick wall blood vessels

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Laparotomy revealed a 12-cm pearly-white multivesicular cyst in the left adrenal gland whose puncture yielded clear hydatid fluid, with subsequent histopathological examination establishing a primary adrenal hydatid cyst despite negative preoperative serology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The puncture of the cyst showed a multivesicular clear content... The final pathological examination of the specimen led to a hydatid cyst of the adrenal gland (Fig. 3).

editor_comments: Primary hydatid cysts of the adrenal gland represent an exceedingly rare localization (<0.5% of cases), typically presenting as an indolent incidentaloma or chronic flank pain. Due to frequent serological negativity in thick-walled or quiescent retroperitoneal cysts, differentiating hydatid disease from non-functioning adrenocortical carcinoma or pheochromocytoma relies on identifying pathognomonic multicystic daughter vesicles and curvilinear calcifications on CT.
